Got Lactose?

  • Lactose is the main sugar found in milk.
  • Lactose intolerance is the inability to properly digest lactose.
  • Lactose intolerance can be addressed by
    • avoiding lactose-containing foods or
    • consuming lactase pills along with food.

Organic Compounds

The cell consists mainly water and carbon-based molecules.

Carbon forms large, complex, and diverse molecules necessary for life’s functions.

Organic compounds are carbon-based molecules.

Carbon Chemistry

  • Carbon is a versatile molecule.
  • The carbon atoms of organic compounds can also bond with other elements, most commonly hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen.
  • Larger organic compounds are the main molecules in gasoline and are important fuels in your body.
Text description of this image

Carbon skeletons vary in length.; The example shows a chain of two carbon atoms joined horizontally by a single bond. Three hydrogen atoms are single bonded to each carbon, drawn above, below, and to the free side of each C.; Carbon skeletons may have double bonds, which can vary in location.; The figure shows the double bond between the first and second carbons in a four-carbon chain. Two hydrogen atoms are also single bonded to the first carbon, one on the left and one above the chain; one H is single bonded above the second carbon; H atoms are single bonded above and below the third carbon; and three H are single bonded above, below, and to the right of the fourth carbon.; Carbon skeletons may be branched or unbranched.; The figure shows that three carbons form a horizontal chain with single bonds between all carbon atoms. Single-bonded above the middle carbon in the chain is a fourth carbon atom. Single-bonded to this carbon atom are three hydrogen atoms, to the left, the right, and above this C. Three hydrogen atoms are also single-bonded to the first and third carbons in the three-carbon chain (above, below, and to the free side of the end carbons). A final H is single-bonded below the middle carbon in the three-carbon chain.; Carbon skeletons may be arranged in rings.; The figure shows a six-carbon ring (forming a hexagon). Double bonds alternate with single bonds between the carbon atoms forming the ring. One hydrogen atom is also single bonded to every carbon atom in the ring.

Text description of this image

Structural formula: The figure shows carbon represented as C and hydrogen as H. A central C is joined by straight lines to four Hs, with all lines (bonds) at right angles.; Ball-and-stick model: The figure shows carbon represented as C and hydrogen as H. A large central ball (C) is joined by sticks to four smaller balls (each are H atoms). The structure forms a pyramid shape.; Space-filling model: A large central sphere is fused to four smaller spheres.

Text description of this image

The examples shown in the figure are as follows:

Octane (represented by a gas can); A space-filling model of octane consists of a chain of carbon and hydrogen atoms.; Dietary fat (represented by a cheeseburger and fries); A space-filling model of octane shows three branches of hydrocarbon chains joined at one end with interspersed oxygen atoms where the chains come together.

  • The unique properties of an organic compound depend on
    • its carbon skeleton and
    • the atoms attached to the skeleton.
  • In an organic compound, the groups of atoms directly involved in chemical reactions are called functional groups.

Building Blocks of Macromolecules

  • Macromolecules are polymers, large molecules made by stringing together many smaller molecules called monomers.
  • A dehydration reaction
    • links two monomers together and
    • removes a molecule of water.
  • The breakdown of polymers occurs by hydrolysis, by adding water to them, a process that is essentially the reverse of a dehydration reaction.

Building - dehydration

Breaking - hydrolysis

Text description of this image

The figure a shows a short polymer consisting of a chain of four monomers. On the ends of the polymer chain are an H atom at one end and a hydroxyl group (OH) at the opposite end. An incoming monomer has the same atoms (H and OH) attached to opposite ends. The hydroxyl group on the short polymer and the H on the monomer are highlighted, as these atoms will come off and form a water molecule (H2O) during the dehydration reaction. The resultant longer polymer consists of a chain of 5 monomers, with an H on one end and an OH on the opposite end of the chain. The figure b shows that an H2O is added to the 5-polymer chain from part (a). During hydrolysis, the polymer is split into two shorter polymers: one is a chain of three monomers and the other is a chain of two monomers. Both shorter polymers have an OH on one end and an H on the opposite end. The OH of the three-monomer chain and the H of the two-monomer chain are highlighted, indicating they came from the water molecule that was added during hydrolysis.

Macromolecules – Large Biological Molecules

Four categories of large biological molecules are found in all living creatures:

  • carbohydrates,
  • lipids,
  • proteins, and
  • nucleic acids.

Carbohydrates

  • Carbohydrates include sugars and polymers of sugar.
  • In animals, carbohydrates are dietary energy and material for organic compounds.
  • In plants, carbohydrates serve as a building material for much of the plant body.
  • Monosaccharides
    • are the monomers of carbohydrates and
    • cannot be broken down into smaller sugars.
  • Common examples are glucose in sports drinks and fructose found in fruit.

Monosaccharides

Text description of this image

Glucose and fructose are isomers, meaning they have the same formula C6H12O6, with different arrangements of the atoms. The figure shows glucose and fructose as vertical chains of six carbon atoms (C), all joined by single bonds. Glucose: The top carbon atom is part of a carbonyl group, which means it is double-bonded to an O. That top C is also single-bonded to H. The second, fourth, fifth and sixth carbons in the glucose chain are also single-bonded to hydroxyl groups (OH) on the right and H atoms on the left; this orientation is reversed for the third C in the glucose chain, which is single-bonded to an OH on the left and an H on the right. The bottom carbon in the chain is also single-bonded to an H below the chain. Fructose: The differences in the arrangement of atoms are with the top two carbons in the six-carbon chain. The top carbon is bonded to a hydroxyl group (OH) on the right and H atoms above the chain and to the left. The second carbon is a carbonyl group and is double-bonded to O. Carbons 3 to 6 are bonded to OH and H in the same way as C3 to C6 in glucose.

Different ways of showing carbohydrates

Text description of this image

The figure shows glucose as a linear vertical chain and also a ring. The details of the linear arrangement are as follows:

Glucose is a 6-carbon chain (here drawn vertically).; The carbons, starting from the top carbon, are numbered C1 to C6 and single bonds join the carbons.; C1 is double-bonded to an O and single-bonded to H. C2, C4, C5 and C6 are all single-bonded to OH on the right and H on the left; this orientation is reversed for C3, which is single-bonded to OH on the left and H on the right.; C6 is also single-bonded to an H below the chain.

The details of the ring structure where glucose forms a hexagon are as follows:

C1 is at the right point of the ring and is single-bonded to H above the ring and OH below.; C2 is in the lower right corner and is single-bonded to H above and OH below.; C3 is in the lower left corner and is single-bonded to OH above and H below the plane of the ring.; C4 is at the left point of the ring and is single-bonded to an H above and an OH below the ring.; C5 is in the upper left corner and is single-bonded to CH2OH above the ring and to H below.; The C in the CH2OH is C6. There is an O in the upper right corner of the ring.

The figure also shows a hexagon ring, with all corners unlabeled except for an O in the upper right corner of the ring. There are no atoms drawn as attached to the ring in this symbol.

Monosaccharides

Disaccharides

Text description of this image

Glucose and fructose are isomers, meaning they have the same formula C6H12O6, with different arrangements of the atoms. The figure shows glucose and fructose as vertical chains of six carbon atoms (C), all joined by single bonds. Glucose: The top carbon atom is part of a carbonyl group, which means it is double-bonded to an O. That top C is also single-bonded to H. The second, fourth, fifth and sixth carbons in the glucose chain are also single-bonded to hydroxyl groups (OH) on the right and H atoms on the left; this orientation is reversed for the third C in the glucose chain, which is single-bonded to an OH on the left and an H on the right. The bottom carbon in the chain is also single-bonded to an H below the chain. Fructose: The differences in the arrangement of atoms are with the top two carbons in the six-carbon chain. The top carbon is bonded to a hydroxyl group (OH) on the right and H atoms above the chain and to the left. The second carbon is a carbonyl group and is double-bonded to O. Carbons 3 to 6 are bonded to OH and H in the same way as C3 to C6 in glucose.

Text description of this image

The figure shows abbreviated ring structures of glucose and galactose.

Glucose is a hexagon ring with an O in the upper right corner and an OH attached below the right point of the ring. This OH is highlighted, indicating it will become part of the water molecule removed during the dehydration reaction.; Galactose is also a hexagon ring with an O in the upper right corner and an O attached below the left point of the ring. Near that O, an H is highlighted, as it will also become part of the water molecule removed as the rings are joined.; After H2O is removed, lactose is formed, consisting of the glucose ring with an O attached below the right point of the ring. Attached to that O is the left point of the galactose ring.

Polysaccharides

  • Starch
  • Glycogen
  • Cellulose
Text description of this image

The three polysaccharides illustrated in the figure are as follows: a) Starch: Starch granules in potato tuber cells (visible in a micrograph as globular structures) have the structure of a long chain of linked glucose monomers. b) Glycogen: Glycogen granules in muscle tissue (from the gardener’s arm) are visible as small dots in a micrograph, and have the structure of branched chains of glucose monomers. c) Cellulose: Cellulose microfibrils, such as those found in the leaves of a potato plant, are visible in a micrograph as a mat of tightly woven fibers. Within each fiber are cellulose molecules, composed of parallel chains of glucose monomers. Hydrogen bonds link the chains.

Lipids

  • Almost all carbohydrates are hydrophilic (“water-loving”) molecules that dissolve readily in water.
  • Lipids are hydrophobic, unable to mix with water.
  • Lipids also differ from carbohydrates, proteins, and nucleic acids in that neither are they huge macromolecules nor are they necessarily polymers built from repeating monomers.
  • Lipids are a diverse group of molecules made from different molecular building blocks.

Fats

  • A typical fat, or triglyceride, consists of a glycerol molecule joined with three fatty acid molecules via a dehydration reaction.
  • Fats perform essential functions in the human body, including
    • energy storage,
    • cushioning, and
    • insulation.
Text description of this image

The figure shows that the structure of glycerol, as a chain of 3 carbons, arranged in a vertical line, with OH single-bonded to the right of each C, and H atoms single-bonded to the left of each C and above or below the top and bottom carbons in the chain.

The fatty acid is a long chain, here drawn in a horizontal line, of 15 CH2s joined by single bonds (the 15th C is a CH3 rather than a CH2).; The first (left) CH2 in the chain is bonded to a carbonyl group (C double-bonded to an O above) on the left.; The C in the carbonyl group is also single-bonded on the left to an OH, which is highlighted to indicate that it will be removed during a dehydration reaction linking the fatty acid to the top carbon in the glycerol.; The top carbon in the glycerol will also lose an H from its attached OH when the fatty acid is joined; thus removing a water molecule as the fatty acid is linked to the glycerol.

The figure shows a glycerol consisting of a three-carbon chain arranged vertically. Each glycerol carbon is single-bonded to an O on the right, which is in turn single-bonded to the carbonyl group at the beginning of a fatty acid chain. Thus, three fatty acids are attached to the glycerol, one to each carbon in the glycerol. Two fatty acid chains are drawn straight, but the third has a kink at the site of a double-bond between carbons. The carbons that are double-bonded are CHs rather than CH2S.

  • If the carbon skeleton of a fatty acid has fewer than the maximum number of hydrogens at the double bond, it is unsaturated.
  • If it has the maximum number of hydrogens, it is saturated.
  • A saturated fat has all three of its fatty acids saturated.
  • Most animal fats have (1) a relatively high proportion of saturated fatty acids, (2) can easily stack, tending to be solid at room temperature, and (3) contribute to atherosclerosis.
  • Most plant and fish fats tend to be (1) high in unsaturated fatty acids and (2) liquid at room temperature.

Types of Fat

Text description of this image

Saturated fats: Unhealthy fats found primarily in meat and full-fat dairy products; solid at room temperature; A photo shows a chocolate ice cream cone.; A photo shows a wedge of Swiss cheese.; A photo shows red meat.; A photo shows three sticks of butter.; Unsaturated fats: Fats found primarily in fish and plants; usually liquid at room temperature; A photo shows bottles of plant and fish oils: They are unhydrogenated and usually liquid at room temperature.; Trans fats: Unhealthy fats in hydrogenated processed foods; solid at room temperature

§ A photo shows a donut. § An exploded view of an ingredients list has fully hydrogenated and partially hydrogenated oils circled.

Omega-3 fats: Beneficial fats in some fish and plant oils; liquid at room temperature

§ A photo shows a salmon steak. § A photo shows green olives. § A photo shows a pile of walnut meat.

Steroids

  • Steroids are very different from fats in structure and function.
    • The carbon skeleton has four fused rings.
    • Steroids vary in the functional groups attached to this set of rings, and these chemical variations affect their function.
  • Cholesterol is
    • a key component of cell membranes and
    • the “base steroid” from which your body produces other steroids, such as estrogen and testosterone.
Text description of this image

Cholesterol:; The structure is based on four fused carbon rings, described here from left to right and drawn based on abbreviated ring structures. (Fused means that the rings share a side). The first ring is a hexagon with the points arranged at the top and the bottom. There is an OH single bonded to the lower left corner. The right side of the first ring is fused to the left side of the second ring, also a hexagon with the points arranged at the top and bottom. Single-bonded above the fused side of these rings is a CH3. Fused to the upper right side of the second ring by its lower left side is the third ring, also a hexagon. Its right side is fused to the left side of the fourth ring, which is a pentagon. Single-bonded above the fused side of the 3rd and 4th rings is another CH3. The point of the pentagon points up. Single-bonded to this point is a carbon chain that has a CH3 on the left and then five zig-zag points before branching to two final CH3 groups. The point of the pentagon is single-bonded to the first zig-zag point in the chain, to the right of the CH3 group.; Testosterone; The structure of is identical to cholesterol, except that on the first ring, there is a double-bond to O from the lower left corner in the place of OH; and single-bonded to the pentagon, in place of the carbon chain in cholesterol, is an OH.; A photo shows a lion with mane.; Estrogen; The structure of is also identical to cholesterol, except that in place of the carbon chain attached to the point of the pentagon, there is a double-bond to O.; A photo shows a lioness without any mane.

Proteins

Text description of this image

Structural proteins: Provide support; Structural proteins form hair, ligaments and horns.; A photo shows a woman with curly hair.; A photo shows a ram with big horns.; Storage proteins: Provide amino acids for growth; Seeds and eggs are rich in storage proteins.; A photo shows seeds coming out of a flower.; A photo shows an egg.; Contractile proteins: Help movement; Contractile proteins enable muscles to contract.; A photo shows a man lifting weights in a gym.; Transport proteins: Help transport substances; The protein hemoglobin within red blood cells transports oxygen.; A micrograph shows a cluster of red blood cells.; Enzymes: Help chemical reactions; Some cleaning products use enzymes to help break down molecules.; A photo shows a bottle with a label that reads, "Natural Earth Enzymes."

Text description of this image

The figure a shows that the structure of an amino acid is such that a central carbon atom is single-bonded on the left to the N in an amino group (an amino group is an N single-bonded to two Hs); to an H above; on the right to the C in a carboxyl group (a carboxyl group is a C double-bonded to O and single-bonded to OH) and to a side chain below and The figure b shows that the structures of leucine and serine are identical except for their side groups.

Leucine; The side group of the amino acid leucine is pure hydrocarbon, making it the hydrophobic side of the chain. The structure of the hydrophobic side group in leucine is a CH2 single-bonded above to the amino acid central carbon. Single-bonded to the C in that CH2 is a CH. A branch of two CH3s are single bonded to the C in the CH.; Serine; The side group of the amino acid serine has a hydroxyl group (-OH), which is hydrophilic.; The structure of serine’s hydrophilic side group is a CH2 single-bonded to the central carbon in the amino acid above. Single-bonded below the CH2 is an OH.

  • Cells link amino acids together by dehydration reactions,
    • forming peptide bonds, and
    • creating long chains of amino acids called polypeptides.
  • A functional protein is one or more polypeptide chains precisely twisted, folded, and coiled into a molecule of unique shape.
Text description of this image

The figure shows that during a dehydration reaction, an OH comes off the carboxyl group of one amino acid and an H is removed from the amino group of a second amino acid, releasing a molecule of water (H2O). The peptide bond formed is between the C in the carboxyl group of the first amino acid and the N in the amino group of the second.

  • The amino acid sequence of each polypeptide determines the three-dimensional structure.
  • A protein’s three-dimensional structure enables the molecule to carry out its specific function.
  • Nearly all proteins work by recognizing and binding to some other molecule.
  • A protein’s shape is sensitive to the environment.
  • An unfavorable change in temperature, pH, or some other factor can cause a protein to unravel.
Text description of this image

An illustration shows the amino acid sequence of lysozyme resembling beads on a string. There are 129 amino acids; the first five are Lysine-Valine-Phenylalanine-Glycine-Arginine. The tenth is ala, which stands for alanine. The chemical structure of alanine is drawn as an example. It is a central C bonded to NH2 on the left, to H above, to COOH on the right, and to CH2 below. The CH2 is also bonded below to OH. A ribbon model shows how the polypeptide folds into its compact shape, with coils or helices in some regions and flat folded sections in others. An illustration shows a detailed protein structure showing the complex three-dimensional shape.

Nucleic Acids

  • Nucleic acids are macromolecules that
    • store information and
    • provide the instructions for building proteins.
  • They consist of two types:
    1. DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid and
    2. RNA (ribonucleic acid).
  • Nucleic acids are polymers made from monomers called nucleotides.
  • Each nucleotide has three parts:
    1. a five-carbon sugar,
    2. a phosphate group, and
    3. a nitrogen-containing base.
Text description of this image

A nucleotide is made up of a phosphate group attached to a sugar (deoxyribose), which is attached to a nitrogenous base (A, G, C, or T).; The phosphate group is drawn as a central P bonded to Os at the left, right, and above and below. The bond to the O on the left is a double bond; all other bonds are single bonds. The O below the central P has a negative charge. The connection to the next nucleotide in the chain (above) is from the O above the central P. From the O to the right of the P there is a single bond to CH2; this is in turn single-bonded to the C at the upper left corner of the sugar.; Deoxyribose sugar is a five-membered ring, viewed on edge with an O at the top point of the pentagon on the far side of the structure. The C in the upper right corner is single-bonded to the nitrogenous base above, and to an H below. The C in the lower right corner is single-bonded to Hs above and below. The C in the lower left corner is single-bonded to H above and to O below; this O is the point of connection to the next nucleotide in the chain (below). The C in the upper left corner is bonded to an H below, and to the CH2 above that connects the sugar to the phosphate. In this example the nitrogenous base attached to the sugar is thymine.; Thymine (T) is a six-membered ring, with nitrogen atoms in the upper right corner and in the bottom point. The first (upper right) nitrogen is single bonded to an H; the second is attached to the sugar as described above. There is a double bond between the carbons in the left of the ring; all other bonds within the ring itself are single bonds. The Cs in the lower right corner and at the top point of the ring both have double-bonds to O. The C in the upper left corner is single-bonded to CH3. The C in the lower left corner is single-bonded to H.; A figure illustrates the symbol used in this book to represent that atomic structure. The symbol shows a small rectangle (phosphate) sitting on top of a larger rectangle (sugar). Attached horizontally to the sugar is a rectangle with a jagged free edge (base).

Nitrogen Bases & DNA Structure

Text description of this image

The detailed nitrogenous base structures as shown in the figure are as follows:

Adenine (A) is composed of fused double rings that include a six-membered ring on the right and a pentagon ring fused to the left side of the hexagon with the point oriented horizontally to the left. There are double bonds between the carbons in the shared side of these rings. There is an N in the upper left corner of the pentagon ring, double-bonded to the C in the point of the pentagon (oriented at the left). The C in the point is single-bonded to an H off the ring, and also single-bonded to another N in the lower left corner of the pentagon ring. That N is single-bonded to an H below the ring and to the bottom C in the shared side of the two fused rings. In the hexagon ring, the points are arranged at the top and the bottom of the ring, and there is a C at the top point and an N at the bottom point. The top C is single-bonded to an N above the ring, which is also single-bonded to two Hs. The top C is also double-bonded to an N in the upper right corner of the hexagon ring, which is single-bonded to the C in the lower right corner; that C is double-bonded to the N at the bottom point of the ring, and single-bonded to an H off the ring.; Guanine (G) is composed of fused double rings that include a six-membered ring on the right and a pentagon ring fused to the left side of the hexagon with the point oriented horizontally to the left. There are double bonds between the carbons in the shared side of these rings. There is an N in the upper left corner of the pentagon ring, double-bonded to the C in the point of the pentagon (oriented at the left). The C in the point is single-bonded to an H off the ring, and also single-bonded to another N in the lower left corner of the pentagon ring. That N is single-bonded to an H below the ring and to the bottom C in the shared side of the two fused rings. In the hexagon ring, the points are arranged at the top and the bottom, and there is a C at the top point and an N at the bottom point. The top C is double-bonded to O, and also single-bonded to an N in the upper right corner of the hexagon. That N is also single bonded to an H off the ring, and single-bonded to the C in the lower right corner. That C is double-bonded to the N at the bottom point of the ring and single-bonded to an N off the ring, which is also single-bonded to two additional Hs.; Thymine (T) is a single-ring structure. It is shown as a hexagon with the points arranged vertically. The atoms that make up the ring are: C in the top point, N in the upper right corner, C in the lower right corner, N at the bottom point, C in the lower left corner, and C in the upper left corner. There is a double bond between the carbons in the left side of the ring and a double bond to O off the ring from the C in the lower right corner. There are single bonds to H off the ring from the N in the bottom point, the C in the lower left corner, and the N in the upper right corner. There is a single bond to CH3 from the C in the upper left corner, and a double bond to O above the ring from the top carbon.; Cytosine (C) is a single-ring hexagon with the points arranged vertically. The atoms that make up the ring are: C in the top point, N in the upper right corner, C in the lower right corner, N at the bottom point, C in the lower left corner, and C in the upper left corner. There is a double bond between the carbons in the left side of the ring and between the top carbon and the N in the upper right corner. There is a double bond to O off the ring from the C in the lower right corner, and single bonds to H off the ring from the N in the bottom point, the C in the lower left corner, and the C in the upper left corner. There is another single bond to N above the ring from the C in the top point. That N is also single-bonded to two additional Hs.

Text description of this image

DNA strand (polynucleotide): The figure shows a sugar-phosphate backbone that repeats sugar-phosphate-sugar-phosphate for the length of the strand. Attached to the sugars are bases: either A, G, T, or C. A and G are long bases while T and C are short. A nucleotide consists of a phosphate, sugar, and base and has been marked.; Double helix (two polynucleotide strands): The figure shows the double helix resembling a twisted ladder with the sugar-phosphate backbones on the outside and the base pairing together to form the rungs of the ladder. A always pairs with T and C always pairs with G through hydrogen bonds.
